metadata.repo_type_justification: Application source with a deployable entry point is present (frmCustomer.frm, a VB6 form with a Form_Load bootstrap compiled into a Win32 EXE per README.md), with no multi-service layout and no resource-provisioning IaC.
metadata.archetype_justification: The form opens an ADODB connection to a Microsoft Access .mdb it owns and performs an INSERT on customer records in cmdSave_Click - owned persistent state with write operations.
metadata.framework: VB6 forms + ADODB (Jet OLEDB 4.0); Crystal Reports 8.5
metadata.surface_flags_rationale: An Access .mdb on an SMB share is a self-managed persistent store with at-rest data. There is no Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifest or AWS-provisioning IaC (deployment is hand-copying the EXE), and no HTTP/gRPC surface - it is a single-user Win32 desktop binary.

classification_consistency_check.reason: Overall score 1.05 falls in the Not Ready band, but only 11 High findings were emitted - one short of the >=12 threshold that would force the Not Ready tier - because 5 questions (INF-Q9, SEC-Q1, OPS-Q5, OPS-Q7, OPS-Q9) were surface-gated to Not Evaluated and emitted no findings. The divergence is an artifact of correct surface gating on a repo with no IaC and no deployed workload, not a scoring error; both lenses agree the system is at the bottom of the maturity range. Documented and flagged for the maintainer rather than corrected, because re-scoring the gated questions would penalize surfaces the repo does not expose.

top_gaps.title: Programming Languages
top_gaps.gap: Visual Basic 6.0 - no AWS SDK, no cloud-native tooling, IDE and runtime unsupported by Microsoft.
top_gaps.impact: Every other pathway is gated on a language migration; no lift-and-shift path exists for a VB6 EXE.

top_gaps.title: Managed Databases
top_gaps.gap: Microsoft Access 2003 .mdb on an SMB file share, documented to corrupt monthly under concurrent writes.
top_gaps.impact: Data loss and multi-user locking failures are active production incidents; blocks all scaling.

top_gaps.title: Secrets Management
top_gaps.gap: Jet OLEDB database password hardcoded as DB_PW = "crm2005pw" in source and compiled into the EXE.
top_gaps.impact: Plaintext credential in version control, distributed to every field laptop with no rotation path.

top_gaps.title: Monolith vs Microservices
top_gaps.gap: UI, data access and SQL all in one form module; no layers, no module boundaries.
top_gaps.impact: Nothing can be extracted or reused; decomposition requires a rewrite rather than extraction.

top_gaps.title: CI/CD Automation
top_gaps.gap: No build server - compiled on one developer's machine and the EXE is copied by hand.
top_gaps.impact: No reproducible build, no rollback, and no way to safely deliver any modernization increment.

pathways.name: Move to AI
pathways.key_trigger_criteria: Contextual guard not satisfied: requires AI/agent/LLM intent evidenced in the repository
pathways.not_triggered_reason: No AI/agent intent evidenced in the repository (no AI-related signal terms in dependencies, source, configuration, IaC, or documentation). frmCustomer.frm and README.md contain no AI, LLM, Bedrock, RAG, embedding or vector-store references, and there is no dependency manifest.

decomposition_strategy.recommendation_rationale: The monolith is not merely coupled - it is written in a language with no AWS SDK and no supported runtime (APP-Q1 = 1), which removes 'keep the code, change the topology' from the option set. Strangler Fig lets the data tier move to Aurora first, with the VB6 client repointed through an ODBC/anti-corruption shim, then screens migrate one at a time with no cutover weekend.

approaches.name: Strengthen as Modular Monolith
approaches.note: Weak fit - the drivers are an unsupported runtime, a corrupting data file and embedded credentials, none of which module boundaries address.

approaches.name: Strangler Fig (Parallel Track)
approaches.note: Keeps field sales working throughout and delivers the highest-risk fix (the .mdb) first.

approaches.name: Conditional / Adaptive
approaches.note: Not available - a Win32 VB6 EXE with a mapped-drive dependency cannot be usefully containerized before it is rewritten.

approaches.name: Big-Bang Rewrite
approaches.note: Recommended against. Plausible given the tiny surface, but no tests and 'last touched 2018' mean undocumented behavior surfaces late.

findings.title: Managed Compute
findings.description: All compute is a Win32 desktop EXE on field-sales laptops under a Windows 10/11 compatibility shim. No aws_ecs_*, aws_eks_*, aws_lambda_*, aws_instance, Dockerfile or Kubernetes manifest exists in the repository.
findings.gap: Zero managed compute; there is no server-side execution tier at all, so elastic scaling, managed patching and centralized deployment are all unavailable.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a server-side tier: expose customer operations through an API on ECS Fargate or Lambda and reduce the desktop client to a thin consumer or replace it with a web client.

findings.title: Managed Databases
findings.description: The operational database is a Microsoft Access 2003 .mdb on an SMB file share opened directly by each client via the Jet OLEDB 4.0 provider (DB_PATH = S:\CRM\sales.mdb). Reporting runs on a self-managed SQL Server 2012 fed by a scheduled DTS/SSIS package. Both are commercial engines; neither is managed.
findings.gap: No managed database, no automated failover and no real concurrency control; README records monthly corruption under concurrent writes and frequent record-locked errors on a single file server with no failover.
findings.recommendation: Migrate to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL (Multi-AZ) as the single operational store and serve reporting from a read replica, retiring the nightly sync. Use AWS SCT for the SQL Server schema and export-and-load for the Access data.

findings.title: Network Security
findings.description: No VPC, subnet, security group or network policy exists in the repository. The owned network surface is a mapped SMB drive (S:\) to a single Windows file server, with every laptop holding direct file-level read/write access to the database file and carrying the database password in its binary.
findings.gap: No network segmentation or tiering: clients have direct filesystem access to the datastore instead of a service boundary, so any compromised laptop has full read/write access to all customer data.
findings.recommendation: Terminate direct client access to the data tier. Place Aurora in private subnets with least-privilege security groups reachable only from the new application tier, and define the topology in IaC.

findings.title: Infrastructure as Code Coverage
findings.description: 0% IaC coverage. A scan for *.tf, *.tfvars, CloudFormation templates, cdk.json, Chart.yaml, kustomization.yaml and Ansible playbooks found none; the repository contains exactly three files. The file share, file server, SQL Server instance and DTS/SSIS schedule are all manually administered.
findings.gap: Nothing is reproducible. The application depends on data-store and networking surfaces with no IaC for either, so environments cannot be rebuilt and disaster recovery has no mechanism.
findings.recommendation: Define the target state in CDK or CloudFormation from the first migration increment - network, database, compute and operational resources - rather than provisioning by hand.

evidence.file: repository root (scanned for *.tf, Dockerfile, .github/workflows/, k8s/, *.sql, tests)

findings.title: CI/CD Automation
findings.description: No pipeline definitions exist: no .github/workflows/, .gitlab-ci.yml, Jenkinsfile, buildspec.yml or appspec.yml. README states the application is compiled on one developer's machine, has no installer, and is deployed by hand-copying the EXE and the .mdb template.
findings.gap: No automated build, test or deploy stage, plus a single-machine build dependency that is a key-person risk - the VB6 IDE needed to produce the binary is itself unsupported.
findings.recommendation: Stand up CodePipeline/CodeBuild as the first modernization increment, before any data-tier change, and capture the build environment explicitly.

findings.title: Monolith vs Microservices
findings.description: A single deployable Win32 EXE with no internal structure. frmCustomer.frm combines presentation (txtName, cmdSave), connection lifecycle (Form_Load, Form_Unload) and persistence (a string-concatenated INSERT in cmdSave_Click) in one form module. No packages, layers, data-access abstraction or module boundaries exist.
findings.gap: Tightly-coupled monolith with pervasive shared state (a module-level cn connection used directly from UI handlers). Nothing is independently testable, deployable or extractable.
findings.recommendation: Follow the Strangler Fig approach: establish the new data tier, place an anti-corruption layer over the legacy schema, then rebuild screens against a service API on a supported runtime.

findings.title: Unstructured Data Storage
findings.description: No aws_s3_bucket, no Textract or parsing call and no object-storage client. The only data surface is a local-network file system: the Access .mdb on the S:\ SMB share plus Crystal Reports 8.5 output, reachable only from the corporate network.
findings.gap: Data including report artifacts sits on legacy file-system storage with no managed object store, so it is not addressable, versioned, lifecycle-managed, or available to analytics or AI workloads.
findings.recommendation: Move report output and document attachments to S3 with versioning and lifecycle policies; S3 File Gateway can bridge the file-share dependency during migration without duplicating data.

findings.title: Database Engine Version and EOL
findings.description: Both engines are past end of life and neither is pinned in any deployment artifact, because no IaC exists. README identifies Microsoft Access 2003 (Jet) operationally and SQL Server 2012 for reporting; frmCustomer.frm binds the deprecated Microsoft.Jet.OLEDB.4.0 provider. Access 2003 support ended in 2014 and SQL Server 2012 in 2022.
findings.gap: Engines at or past EOL with no version pinning and no upgrade path - no security patches are available for either, and the Jet OLEDB 4.0 provider is unavailable on 64-bit runtimes, constraining in-place modernization.
findings.recommendation: Treat engine EOL as the forcing function for the Managed Databases pathway: migrate to Aurora PostgreSQL with an explicitly pinned engine version in IaC and a documented upgrade procedure covering downtime and rollback.

findings.title: Encryption at Rest
findings.description: Surface flag has_at_rest_data_surface=true (the .mdb on the SMB share is a real at-rest surface). No encryption at rest is configured - no aws_kms_key, no kms_key_id, no disk- or file-level encryption. The only protection on the customer data file is the Jet database password crm2005pw, an obfuscation mechanism rather than encryption and trivially recoverable from the .mdb.
findings.gap: Customer PII sits unencrypted in a file on a network share protected only by a shared static Jet password that is also embedded in every distributed binary; anyone with SMB read access to S:\CRM\ can copy and open the whole database.
findings.recommendation: Restrict share ACLs and enable volume-level encryption on the file server as immediate mitigation; at migration use customer-managed KMS keys on Aurora and S3 with a documented rotation policy.

findings.title: Secrets Management
findings.description: A plaintext production credential is committed to source: Private Const DB_PW As String = "crm2005pw", concatenated into the connection string as Jet OLEDB:Database Password=. README independently confirms the credential is compiled into the distributed EXE. No Secrets Manager, Vault, parameter store or environment indirection is used.
findings.gap: Plaintext credential in version control and in every distributed binary, shared by all users, with no rotation mechanism - rotating it would require recompiling and hand-redistributing the EXE, which is why it is unchanged since 2005.
findings.recommendation: Treat the credential as compromised and rotate it as part of the data-tier migration; store the new credential in AWS Secrets Manager with automated rotation, retrieved at runtime by the service tier. Note the committed value remains in git history.

findings.title: Integration Testing
findings.description: There are no tests of any kind in the repository - no test directory, no test files, and no CI to run them in. README states this directly under Known Issues: no tests, no build server.
findings.gap: No automated tests at all, the single largest risk multiplier for this modernization: there is no regression safety net for a database migration, a language rewrite or a credential rotation.
findings.recommendation: Before changing the data tier, write characterization tests for the customer-save path including the failure modes the message box currently hides, and run them in CI. This is the prerequisite that makes Strangler Fig safe.

findings.title: Workflow Orchestration
findings.description: Archetype-calibrated (stateful-crud rubric applied). The only multi-step process - the nightly ETL into the reporting database - is a scheduled DTS/SSIS package with no orchestration service, no retry policy and no state tracking. No aws_sfn_*, Temporal or workflow definition exists.
findings.gap: A business-critical multi-step data movement runs with no orchestration, no error handling and no observable run state; a failed nightly sync is invisible until reports are wrong.
findings.recommendation: Re-implement the sync as an AWS Step Functions state machine, or remove the need for it entirely by serving reporting from an Aurora read replica (preferred).

findings.title: Async Messaging and Streaming
findings.description: Archetype-calibrated (stateful-crud rubric applied; the Score-4 bar for this archetype is managed messaging for cross-boundary state changes). No messaging or streaming infrastructure exists - no aws_sqs_*, aws_sns_*, aws_kinesis_*, aws_msk_*, aws_eventbridge_* and no broker clients. Customer state reaches the reporting database by nightly batch.
findings.gap: State changes crossing a data-store boundary propagate once a day by batch, giving a 24-hour consistency window and no event signal on write.
findings.recommendation: Emit customer change events to EventBridge from the new service tier, or eliminate cross-boundary propagation with a read replica. Do not introduce Kafka/MSK - volumes do not justify it.

findings.title: API Entry Point
findings.description: No API Gateway, AppSync, ALB or CloudFront configuration exists, and there is no HTTP surface to front. The client reaches the database directly over SMB/OLEDB with no intermediary.
findings.gap: No single point of control for authentication, throttling or request validation, because there is no service entry point at all.
findings.recommendation: Introduce Amazon API Gateway in front of the new service tier with request validation, throttling and a Cognito or corporate-IdP authorizer.

findings.title: Auto-Scaling
findings.description: No aws_autoscaling_* or aws_appautoscaling_* resources and no scaling configuration of any kind. Capacity is fixed by the number of laptops and one file server; the Access engine has no scaling model.
findings.gap: Capacity is entirely static and the shared-file concurrency ceiling is already being hit, surfacing as record-lock errors and file corruption rather than graceful degradation.
findings.recommendation: After migration, configure target-tracking auto-scaling on the ECS service and Aurora replica auto-scaling for the reporting read path.

findings.title: Backup and Recovery
findings.description: No backup configuration exists - no aws_backup_plan, no retention setting, no snapshot policy and no documented restore procedure. The datastore is a single .mdb on a single file server that README reports corrupting roughly monthly.
findings.gap: A data store with a known monthly corruption rate has no defined backup, no point-in-time recovery and no tested restore.
findings.recommendation: Institute versioned off-server copies of the .mdb as interim mitigation, and at migration enable Aurora automated backups with PITR plus a rehearsed restore runbook.

findings.title: Programming Languages
findings.description: The sole language is Visual Basic 6.0 (frmCustomer.frm: VERSION 5.00, Begin VB.Form, ADODB), with Crystal Reports 8.5 for reporting. README confirms the VB6 IDE and runtime are unsupported by Microsoft. There is no dependency manifest of any kind.
findings.gap: VB6 sits in the Score-1 band: no AWS SDK, effectively no cloud-native tooling and an unsupported toolchain. The Crystal Reports 8.5 runtime can no longer be installed on current machines.
findings.recommendation: Plan a language migration as the enabling step for every other pathway; target a runtime with first-class AWS SDK support (modern .NET 8+ is the shortest conceptual move from VB6).

findings.title: Async vs Sync Communication
findings.description: Archetype-calibrated (stateful-crud rubric applied - the Score-4 bar here is managed messaging for cross-service state propagation, so sync-only is a genuine gap rather than correct-by-design as it would be for a stateless-utility). All work is synchronous and blocking: cn.Execute runs inline on the UI thread, and the only cross-boundary propagation is a nightly batch.
findings.gap: No async pattern anywhere. The UI blocks on a network-filesystem write whose failure mode is a lock error, and cross-store propagation is a 24-hour batch.
findings.recommendation: In the rebuilt tier keep reads synchronous but publish customer change events asynchronously via EventBridge, removing the nightly batch.

findings.title: Long-Running Process Handling
findings.description: Archetype-calibrated (stateful-crud rubric applied; the bar is that operations over 30 seconds run as async jobs with status polling). Every operation is synchronous regardless of duration - the save path blocks the UI thread and the nightly ETL has no status surface, checkpointing or resumability. No background job framework or job-status mechanism exists.
findings.gap: All operations synchronous regardless of duration. On a contended SMB share the blocking write can stall the UI indefinitely, and the only recovery offered is a Try again message box.
findings.recommendation: Move the ETL to Step Functions (or retire it), and in the rebuilt client make any variable-latency operation an async job with a pollable status endpoint.

findings.title: API Versioning Strategy
findings.description: No versioning of any kind. There is no API surface to version (no OpenAPI, AsyncAPI or GraphQL spec in the repository) and the de facto contract - the Access table schema every laptop binds to directly - is unversioned, so a schema change breaks every deployed EXE simultaneously.
findings.gap: The integration contract is a raw database schema with no versioning and no backward-compatibility guarantee, while clients are updated by hand, so client and schema versions drift uncontrollably.
findings.recommendation: Introduce an explicit versioned API (/v1/) as the contract when the service tier is built so legacy and new clients can coexist during the migration.

findings.title: Service Discovery
findings.description: The datastore location is a compile-time constant: Private Const DB_PATH As String = "S:\CRM\sales.mdb", with a source comment instructing maintainers not to change it because field laptops are mapped to S:\. There is no service registry, no mesh and not even environment-variable indirection.
findings.gap: All endpoints hard-coded in application code and baked into a hand-distributed binary - relocating the database requires recompiling and redistributing the EXE to every laptop.
findings.recommendation: Externalize connection configuration immediately, then use AWS Cloud Map / ECS Service Connect for service resolution in the rebuilt tier.

findings.title: Unified Data Access Layer
findings.description: There is no data access layer. The ADODB connection is built inline in the Form_Load UI handler, held in a module-level cn variable, and SQL is executed directly from cmdSave_Click. No repository, DAO or ORM abstraction exists and the connection string is assembled from in-source constants.
findings.gap: Database access is embedded in UI event handlers with no pattern and no single point of data contract - there is nowhere to enforce parameterization, retry, pooling or auditing.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a repository layer in the rebuilt application so connection management, parameterized queries and retry policy live in one place; this is also the natural home for the anti-corruption layer.

findings.title: Stored Procedures and Schema Complexity
findings.description: No .sql files, CREATE PROCEDURE, CREATE TRIGGER or CREATE FUNCTION definitions exist, so there is no stored-procedure estate in the application code. Business logic is nonetheless coupled to engine-specific constructs: the INSERT uses the Jet/Access function Now() for CreatedOn, and the nightly transformation into the reporting schema is owned entirely by an out-of-repository DTS/SSIS package.
findings.gap: Moderate proprietary-SQL coupling plus an undocumented, un-versioned SSIS transformation that is not in source control at all; the logic must be rediscovered before it can be migrated.
findings.recommendation: Reverse-engineer the DTS/SSIS package into version-controlled code before migrating, replace Now() with application-supplied timestamps, and use AWS SCT to assess the SQL Server schema. Prefer re-expressing the transformation in the application or Glue over a like-for-like ETL port.

findings.title: API Authentication
findings.description: There is no per-request authentication and no authorization check in the code path. cmdSave_Click writes using the single shared Jet database password for all users and records the actor from the untrusted client-side Environ("USERNAME"), which the user controls and which is never verified. Data access is governed solely by reachability of the S:\ share.
findings.gap: No authentication of the caller and no attributable identity: the CreatedBy audit column comes from a spoofable client-side value, so write attribution cannot be trusted.
findings.recommendation: Introduce an authenticated API tier (API Gateway with OAuth2/JWT via Cognito or the corporate IdP) and derive CreatedBy server-side from the validated token.

findings.title: Centralized Identity Integration
findings.description: No identity provider integration exists - no aws_cognito_*, no OIDC or SAML configuration, no federation. Identity is implicit: the app trusts the Windows session name from Environ("USERNAME") for attribution and uses one shared database credential for access. There is no SSO, group-based authorization or central revocation path.
findings.gap: The application assumes its own identity entirely with no external IdP; revoking a departing employee's access requires removing file-share access, and the embedded database password cannot be revoked per-user at all.
findings.recommendation: Federate with the corporate IdP through Amazon Cognito (or direct OIDC/SAML) during the rebuild so access is centrally granted, audited and revocable.

findings.title: Compute Hardening and Patching
findings.description: No patching strategy and no vulnerability scanning exist - no SSM Patch Manager config, no Inspector or Snyk, no hardened base image, no dependabot.yml or renovate.json. The runtime itself cannot be patched: README records the VB6 IDE and runtime unsupported, both database engines past EOL, and the Crystal Reports 8.5 runtime no longer installable.
findings.gap: No evidence of a patching strategy, on a stack where several components no longer receive vendor security patches at all; the exposure cannot be closed by patching, only by replacing components.
findings.recommendation: Accept that hardening requires replacement: during migration run on managed/patched compute (Fargate or SSM-managed instances), enable Amazon Inspector, and add dependency scanning to the new pipeline.

findings.title: Application Security Pipeline
findings.description: There is no pipeline, therefore no security validation step: no SAST, no dependency scanning, no container scanning, and no Dependabot or Renovate config at any canonical path. This matters concretely - the code contains a textbook SQL injection (txtName.Text concatenated into an INSERT) and a hardcoded secret, both of which a basic SAST or secret-scanning gate would flag.
findings.gap: No automated security scanning of any kind, which is why two high-severity defects (string-concatenated SQL and a committed credential) have persisted in source since at least 2018.
findings.recommendation: Add secret scanning and SAST to the new CodeBuild pipeline with a blocking gate on critical findings, and parameterize the INSERT as part of the rebuild - the current statement is directly injectable via the customer-name field.

findings.title: Distributed Tracing
findings.description: No tracing instrumentation exists - no OpenTelemetry, no X-Ray, no correlation-ID propagation. There is in fact no logging at all: cmdSave_Click and Form_Unload both use On Error Resume Next, so failures are either shown once in a message box or silently discarded with Err.Clear.
findings.gap: No tracing and no error telemetry. Failed writes are invisible to operators - the swallowed-error pattern means a save failing for any reason other than the one the message box names leaves no record anywhere.
findings.recommendation: Instrument the rebuilt service tier with OpenTelemetry/X-Ray end to end, and as an interim step replace On Error Resume Next with explicit handling that writes to a durable log.

findings.title: SLO Definitions
findings.description: Evaluated because has_persistent_data_store=true. No SLO definitions, no CloudWatch alarms, no latency or error-rate thresholds and no monitoring artifacts exist in the repository, so there is nothing from which an implicit SLO could be inferred. Service levels are described only informally as corruption roughly monthly and lock errors common.
findings.gap: No formal definition of acceptable service levels and no monitoring to measure against one, despite documented recurring failures; there is no way to tell whether reliability is improving or degrading.
findings.recommendation: Define SLOs for the customer-save path (availability, write success rate) and for reporting data freshness, then implement them as CloudWatch alarms with error budgets once the workload is on AWS.

findings.title: Business Metrics
findings.description: No custom metrics are published - no put_metric_data equivalent, no telemetry emission, no dashboards. The only business visibility is Crystal Reports 8.5 running against data up to 24 hours stale, with no operational counters such as customers created or save failures.
findings.gap: No custom metrics; business visibility is limited to day-old batch reports, so failure rates and usage patterns are unmeasured.
findings.recommendation: Emit business-outcome metrics (customers created, save success/failure, sync freshness) to CloudWatch from the new service tier and surface them in a QuickSight or CloudWatch dashboard.

findings.title: Anomaly Detection and Alerting
findings.description: No alerting is configured - no CloudWatch alarms, no anomaly detection, no PagerDuty/OpsGenie integration. The alerting mechanism in practice is the end user: a failed save produces a MsgBox telling the salesperson to try again, and nothing is reported to anyone operating the system.
findings.gap: No alerting configured at all. Mean time to detection for both the recurring corruption and a failed nightly sync is bounded only by how long it takes a user to complain.
findings.recommendation: Add CloudWatch alarms on write error rate and sync freshness, with anomaly detection on critical paths once a baseline exists, routed to an on-call channel rather than to the end user.

findings.title: Observability Ownership
findings.description: No observability assets exist to own - no dashboards, no alarms, no SLO files and no CODEOWNERS. Ownership of the application is recorded only in a source comment: Author: Greg P., 2005. Last touched 2018.
findings.gap: No observability ownership and no named owner in any structured form; monitoring is entirely reactive (user complaints) and the only ownership signal is a years-stale code comment.
findings.recommendation: Add a CODEOWNERS file naming the owning team now, and attribute dashboards, alarms and SLOs to that team as they are created during migration.

evaluations.title: High Availability and Fault Isolation
